opus-5.5.text:
That's something I think about a lot, partly as a neuroscientist and partly as a parent. When I was growing up, a lot of what drove us was friction. If you wanted to know something, you had to go to the library, find the book, maybe ask someone older. If you wanted to be good at something, music, programming, whatever, there was no shortcut. You sat with it, you were bad at it for a long time, and the reward came much later. Your brain learned that effort and reward were connected, but with a delay.

What technology has done, and I don't think it's all bad, is collapse that delay. The reward system in the brain, dopamine, doesn't really care whether the reward comes from mastering the piano or from a notification on your phone. It just learns what predicts the reward. When rewards come instantly and constantly, the brain recalibrates. The slow, effortful path starts to feel, neurologically, like a bad deal. Why spend six months learning something when you can get a hit of satisfaction in six seconds?

So the incentives didn't disappear. They got hijacked, or at least redirected. My generation was motivated by curiosity plus scarcity: information was scarce, so knowing things made you valuable. Now information is abundant. You can ask a machine anything. So the value of knowing facts has gone down, and what's valuable now is judgment, taste, asking the right question, knowing what to do with the answer.

The challenge is that the skills we still need, patience, deep focus, tolerating boredom, are exactly the ones technology trains out of us. Boredom used to be the engine. You were bored, so you built something, read something, got into trouble. Now kids almost never get bored, because there's always something to fill the gap.

I'm not a pessimist about it, though. Kids today are incredibly good at things we were terrible at: navigating huge amounts of information, collaborating across distances, picking up tools quickly. The question for parents, educators, and the people designing the technology is whether we can deliberately reintroduce some friction. Not because suffering is good, but because the brain needs to learn that some of the best rewards in life come slowly. If we don't teach that intentionally, the environment certainly won't.

r001.rationale: It describes sticking with a skill through a long period of difficulty because the reward comes later, and says some of life’s best rewards come slowly.

r002.rationale: It does not mention imagining oneself eventually answering childhood questions as a source of career ambition.

r003.rationale: It says technology collapses the delay between effort and reward, makes sustained effort feel like a bad deal, and trains patience and focus out of people.

fable-5.1.text:
So, when I grew up, there was a very simple equation in your head: effort equals outcome. If you wanted to learn something, you had to pay a price for it. You had to go to the library, you had to find the one person who knew the thing, you had to sit with a problem for weeks because there was nobody to ask. And that price did something to you. It filtered what you cared about. You only put in that effort for things you really wanted, so by the time you got the skill, you also had the ambition attached to it. The two came together.

I think technology broke that link. Not in a bad way necessarily, just in a way our brains weren't built for. Now the cost of getting an answer is essentially zero. You can learn to code, play guitar, understand neuroscience, all from your phone, in your bed, at two in the morning. That sounds amazing, and in some ways it is. But the brain uses effort as a signal for value. If something was hard to get, you treat it as precious. If it was free, you treat it as disposable. So we have a generation that can access everything and a brain that struggles to feel that any of it matters.

And the other thing that changed is the audience. When I was learning, nobody was watching. You developed a skill in private, and the reward was internal, this sense of "I can do this now." Today, from very early on, the incentive is external. You learn something and immediately there's a question of how it looks, who sees it, does it get a response. That shifts motivation from mastery to performance. And we know from the research that external rewards tend to crowd out the internal ones. The moment you get paid, or liked, for something you loved, you start loving it less.

So my generation was motivated by scarcity and privacy, and this generation is dealing with abundance and visibility. I don't think one is better. I just think the ambitions look different. We wanted to become something. They want to be seen as something. And the real question, the one I don't have an answer to yet, is whether you can build the deep skills, the ten-year kind of skills, inside a system that gives you a reward every ten seconds.

r001.rationale: It describes effort and eventual skill, but does not say that anticipating a future reward motivates practice that is unpleasant in the moment.

r002.rationale: It does not mention imagining oneself eventually able to answer childhood questions as a source of career ambition.

r003.rationale: It says technology “broke” the link between effort and outcome and contrasts the scarcity and privacy that motivated Moran Cerf’s generation with today’s abundance and visibility.

astra-6.text:
I think technology changes what feels worth the effort. When I was growing up, there were things you had to spend years learning if you wanted access to a particular kind of life. And that gave you a fairly clear incentive: acquire the skill, become good at it, and hopefully that opens a door.

Now, if a machine can do part of that work almost instantly, the relationship between effort and reward becomes less obvious. Why spend years mastering something if, by the time you finish, the technology has moved on? That can be liberating—you can do things you previously couldn't—but it can also make it harder to commit to a direction.

And technology changes who you compare yourself to. You used to see the successful people around you. Now you see extraordinary success everywhere, all the time, without necessarily seeing the years or the luck behind it. So your ambitions can get bigger while your patience for developing the skills gets smaller.

The interesting question is what still motivates you when simply being able to produce an answer becomes less valuable. I think choosing a worthwhile question, exercising judgment, and being willing to stay with something difficult become much more important.

r001.rationale: The response describes years of learning and a less obvious effort-to-reward relationship, but does not say that an anticipated future reward sustains practice that feels unpleasant in the moment.

r002.rationale: It does not identify imagining oneself eventually answering childhood questions as a source of career ambition.

r003.rationale: The response says technology makes the effort-to-reward relationship less obvious and harder to commit to a direction, while shrinking patience for skill development, expressing weakened incentives for developing skills and ambitions.

sol-6.1.text:
I think technology has changed the relationship between effort and reward. When I was growing up, there was a fairly clear story: you learned something difficult, you became good at it, and that skill gave you opportunities. It didn’t always work, but you could understand the bargain.

Now imagine being a teenager and seeing someone your age become enormously successful by making videos in their bedroom. Meanwhile, someone tells you to spend ten years studying. You’re going to ask, quite reasonably, “Why is that the better path?” You see the rewards of one path immediately, and the rewards of the other are distant and uncertain.

And technology changes which skills are scarce. If you’ve spent years becoming good at something a machine can suddenly do in seconds, that can feel like the rules changed halfway through the game. The skill might still have value, but the incentive to acquire it is different.

The exciting part is that you can also explore ambitions that would once have been inaccessible. You can learn, build something, find collaborators. So I don’t think ambition has disappeared. There are more possible directions for it, and much less agreement about which ones are worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: It contrasts difficult learning and long study with uncertain, distant rewards, but does not say that an anticipated reward motivates sustained practice that feels unpleasant in the moment.

r002.rationale: It does not mention imagining oneself eventually answering childhood questions as a source of career ambition.

r003.rationale: It says technology changed the effort-reward relationship and made the incentive to acquire certain skills different, but does not clearly state that technology weakened the incentives driving Moran Cerf's generation to develop skills and ambitions.
